units.title: Unit 83 — Get: uses, phrases and phrasal verbs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 172–173 (PDF pages 173–174).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: High-frequency verbs, polysemy and phrasal verbs
learningObjectives: Distinguish get meaning obtain, receive, buy, arrive, become, fetch and answer a call or door.
Use get + object + past participle for completing a task or arranging a service.
Use get in touch, get together, get to know and get rid of in appropriate contexts.
Understand get in and get out in different contexts, including arriving by train.
Choose get-related expressions to discuss change, sleep, mistakes and returning objects.

items.pt: conseguir um ingresso; obter uma passagem
items.section: A · Get: obtain, receive and buy
items.example: We managed to get tickets for Saturday’s concert.
items.note: Get can mean obtain something, whether by asking, paying or another means.

items.section: A · Get: obtain, receive and buy
items.example: If the instructions are confusing, get some help from a colleague.
items.note: In this sense, get means obtain or find assistance.

items.section: A · Get: obtain, receive and buy
items.example: I got an email from the school this morning.
items.note: Here get means receive, not necessarily open or read.

items.pt: ganhar um presente; receber um presente
items.section: A · Get: obtain, receive and buy
items.example: She got a lovely present from her grandparents.
items.note: Receive is the relevant meaning; get can also mean buy in another context.

items.section: A · Get: obtain, receive and buy
items.example: I will get a magazine at the station before boarding.
items.note: In a shop or other retail context, get can mean buy.

items.pt: comprar ou ganhar um celular novo
items.section: A · Get: obtain, receive and buy
items.example: I am planning to get a new phone next month.
items.note: Depending on the context, get can mean buy or receive.

items.section: A · Get: obtain, receive and buy
items.example: They could not get a hotel room because every place was full.
items.note: Exercise-derived obtain sense; get here means secure a booking, not receive a room as a gift.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: Text me when you get home safely.
items.note: Here get means arrive. No to is used before home.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: What time did you get here this morning?
items.note: Get + here means arrive here; do not add to before here.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: The room is getting cold because the window is open.
items.note: Get + adjective describes a change of state: become cold.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: It gets dark early during the winter.
items.note: Impersonal it + get + adjective describes daylight changing.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: He got angry when he found his bicycle was missing.
items.note: Get + adjective means become; in this context, become angry.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: I get hungry if I skip breakfast.
items.note: A change of physical state; exercise target using getting + adjective.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: It can get very hot in this office during summer.
items.note: Get + adjective describes a change; hot can refer to a person or place.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: It is getting late, so we should leave soon.
items.note: Typically used with impersonal it: It is getting late.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: Could you go and get my bag from the bedroom?
items.note: Fetch: go to another place and bring the item back.

items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: Could you get the phone while I wash my hands?
items.note: In this context, get means answer a ringing phone.

items.pt: atender a porta; ver quem está na porta
items.section: A · Get: arrive, become, fetch and answer
items.example: Someone is knocking; I will get the door.
items.note: Here get means answer the door, not acquire it.

items.pt: conseguir terminar algo; mandar fazer algo
items.section: A · Get + object + past participle
items.example: We need to get the repairs done before Monday.
items.note: Get + object + past participle can mean completing a task or arranging for another person to do it.

items.pt: cortar o cabelo; mandar cortar o cabelo
items.section: A · Get + object + past participle
items.example: I need to get my hair cut before the wedding.
items.note: Get + object + past participle commonly describes having a professional do a service.

items.section: A · Get + object + past participle
items.example: She got her watch repaired at a small shop near home.
items.note: This causative construction focuses on arranging or obtaining a completed repair.

items.pt: conseguir terminar uma redação; concluir um texto
items.section: A · Get + object + past participle
items.example: I hope to get my essay finished by Thursday.
items.note: Get + object + past participle also means successfully finish a task yourself.

items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: Please get in touch with the organiser if you have questions.
items.note: Make contact, by phone, email, message or another method. The usual pattern is get in touch with someone.

items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: I could not get to sleep because the neighbours were noisy.
items.note: Means begin sleeping; distinct from get up, which means leave bed.

items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: Our old friends get together once a month for dinner.
items.note: People meet and spend time together, often socially.

items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: I got the date wrong and arrived a day too early.
items.note: Get + object + wrong means give, write or understand an incorrect answer or detail.

items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: The weather is getting worse, so let us stay inside.
items.note: Describes a negative change; the opposite is get better.

items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: Her English is getting better with regular practice.
items.note: Describes improvement; contrasts with get worse.

items.pt: livrar-se de algo; desfazer-se de algo
items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: We should get rid of those broken chairs.
items.note: Remove something by throwing it away, selling it or giving it away. Use get rid of + object.

items.pt: conhecer alguém aos poucos; passar a conhecer alguém
items.section: B · Get: fixed phrases
items.example: I got to know my neighbours after moving to the area.
items.note: Get to know describes the process of becoming familiar with someone, not meeting them just once.

items.section: C · Get: phrasal verbs and different meanings
items.example: The door was stuck and we could not get out.
items.note: Leave a car, building or another enclosed place; may imply difficulty.

items.pt: receber algo de volta; recuperar algo
items.section: C · Get: phrasal verbs and different meanings
items.example: I finally got my favourite book back from my cousin.
items.note: Receive the return of something that was lent, lost or taken.

items.section: C · Get: phrasal verbs and different meanings
items.example: We could not get in because the entrance was locked.
items.note: Meaning: enter, especially when access is difficult. Distinct from get in meaning arrive.

items.section: C · Get: phrasal verbs and different meanings
items.example: Our train got in after midnight.
items.note: Meaning: arrive at the destination, particularly for trains and other transport.

items.section: C · Get: phrasal verbs and different meanings
items.example: I usually get up at half past six on weekdays.
items.note: Means rise from bed; waking up and getting up do not always happen at the same time.

sectionsChecked: Exercises 83.1–83.5, including synonyms, changes of state, rewriting and causative constructions

units.title: Unit 84 — Go: meanings and expressions
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 174–175 (PDF pages 175–176).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: High-frequency verbs, activities and state changes
learningObjectives: Use go + -ing and go (out) for a + noun to describe leisure activities.
Describe changes in appearance, ability or mood with go + adjective.
Use go when describing where transport or a route leads, and recognise go meaning disappear.
Distinguish go on, go out, go away, go back and go for in context.
Talk naturally about success, problems and casual greetings using go well, go badly, go wrong and How’s it going?

items.section: A · Go + -ing: leisure activities
items.example: We usually go shopping for groceries on Saturday.
items.note: Use go + -ing to describe an activity; not go to shopping.

items.section: A · Go + -ing: leisure activities
items.example: They went sightseeing during their weekend in Prague.
items.note: Go + -ing describes visiting sights and places of interest.

items.section: A · Go + -ing: leisure activities
items.example: We go swimming at the local pool on Tuesdays.
items.note: Go + -ing commonly describes sport and leisure activities.

items.pt: sair para dançar em casas noturnas; ir a baladas
items.section: A · Go + -ing: leisure activities
items.example: My friends sometimes go clubbing after dinner on Fridays.
items.note: Informal leisure activity: go to nightclubs, usually to dance.

items.pt: sair para caminhar; dar uma caminhada
items.section: A · Go (out) for a + noun
items.example: We like to go for a walk by the river in the evening.
items.note: Go for a walk and go out for a walk are both natural.

items.pt: sair para dar uma volta de carro
items.section: A · Go (out) for a + noun
items.example: They went for a drive along the coast.
items.note: This usually means driving for pleasure rather than for necessary transport.

items.section: A · Go (out) for a + noun
items.example: Would you like to go for a drink after class?
items.note: Go out for a drink is equally natural; the drink need not be alcoholic.

items.pt: sair para fazer uma refeição; comer fora
items.section: A · Go (out) for a + noun
items.example: We went out for a meal to celebrate her promotion.
items.note: Usually implies eating away from home, such as at a restaurant.

items.section: A · Go (out) for a + noun
items.example: We decided to go for a picnic when the sun came out.
items.note: Go (out) for a picnic describes leaving home to eat outdoors.

items.pt: ficar grisalho; ficar com cabelos brancos
items.section: A · Go + adjective: changes of state
items.example: My father started to go grey in his thirties.
items.note: Go + adjective can describe a gradual change, especially an unwanted one. British spelling: grey.

items.section: A · Go + adjective: changes of state
items.example: He is going bald, although he is still quite young.
items.note: Go bald describes losing hair from the head; illustrated in the teaching page.

items.section: A · Go + adjective: changes of state
items.example: Without treatment, the animal could gradually go deaf.
items.note: Describes becoming unable to hear; avoid using as a casual synonym for not listening.

items.section: A · Go + adjective: changes of state
items.example: The old dog is slowly going blind.
items.note: Describes losing the ability to see; an exercise reinforces this phrase.

items.pt: ficar furioso; perder a cabeça de raiva
items.section: A · Go + adjective: changes of state
items.example: Dad will go mad if he finds paint on the new carpet.
items.note: Informal in the lesson: become very angry. Do not assume the speaker means a medical condition.

items.pt: ir até a estação; levar até a estação (rota ou transporte)
items.section: A · Go: routes, disappearance and fetching
items.example: Does this bus go to the station?
items.note: With routes and public transport, go to identifies where the service leads.

items.pt: passar pelo vilarejo; atravessar o povoado
items.section: A · Go: routes, disappearance and fetching
items.example: The road goes through the village before reaching the coast.
items.note: A road or route can go through a place, even though the road itself does not move.

items.section: A · Go: routes, disappearance and fetching
items.example: The money was on the table, but now it has gone.
items.note: Go can mean disappear or no longer be present; past participle: gone.

items.pt: ir buscar; ir pegar e trazer
items.section: A · Go: routes, disappearance and fetching
items.example: Please go and get the coats from the car.
items.note: A common, natural alternative to fetch: go somewhere and bring something back.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: What’s going on outside? I can hear people shouting.
items.note: Go on here means happen or take place, not continue moving.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: Nobody understood what was going on during the meeting.
items.note: This sense of go on means happen. Distinguished from continuing to another step.

items.pt: as luzes se apagam; faltar luz
items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: The lights went out halfway through the performance.
items.note: Go out can mean stop shining or operating, especially of lights.

items.word: go on to the next place
items.pt: seguir para o próximo lugar; prosseguir para outra etapa
items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: After the museum, we went on to the art gallery.
items.note: Go on to something means continue to a further place, topic or activity.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: The interview went well and she received an offer.
items.note: Describes a successful event or activity; opposite: go badly.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: The presentation went badly because the projector failed.
items.note: Describes an unsuccessful event; opposite: go well.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: Something went wrong with the booking, so we lost our reservation.
items.note: Used when problems occur or a plan fails; not simply the opposite of go right in all contexts.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: We are going away for a week at the end of August.
items.note: In the source dialogue, go away means leave home for a holiday, not tell someone to leave.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: We enjoyed Portugal so much that we want to go back next year.
items.note: Return to a place previously visited; often followed by to + destination.

items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: I think I will go for the vegetarian pasta.
items.note: Go for means choose when selecting an option, especially in informal conversation.

items.pt: Como vão as coisas?; Como você está?
items.section: B · Go: phrasal verbs and everyday expressions
items.example: Hi, Ella, how’s it going at your new job?
items.note: An informal greeting that asks how someone or something is doing.
